Interviewer:	Ok, I’ll start off telling you a bit about what we’re doing and the reasons for doing it. The project that we’re working on, we’re mainly interviewing engineers but we decided to use Design & Technology students as well, partly because I think you do quite a bit of engineering within your course and also we’re looking at engineering because it’s a male dominated area and Design & Technology obviously is as well. The project is trying to improve the situation for women within the field of engineering and particularly improving retention of women. A lot of information is now saying that more women are going into the industry but then they leave after a while, so we’re interviewing people about what they expect to get from the industry and then seeing if that changes with time. And then we’re going to put together a guidance document and give it to the Engineering Council and hopefully it will make the situation better for women. So I’ll start off asking you some background questions about why you decided to do Design and things like that. It’s industrial design and technology that you’re doing isn’t it?

Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you do ‘A’ levels?

I did ‘A’ level Design & Technology.

Interviewer:	And what other ‘A’ levels did you do?

I did Geography and Physics.

Interviewer:	OK, and what type of school did you go to?

I went to a girls’ school – a private school.

Interviewer:	Have you got any previous work experience, in the industry?

Not really. Well I did erm two weeks work experience after my GCSE’s, where I worked in an Architect’s office. (OK) So it’s not really the same as design but it’s kind of technical.

Interviewer:	OK, what do your parents do? Are either of them in the industry at all?

No, my dad’s just a business man. I don’t really know what he does. Erm, my mum she works in a big cash and carry – she does administration.

Interviewer:	OK, when and why then do you think that you decided to do Design and Technology?

Well, you do like a bit of Design Technology like – at my school you do it in like – from Year 7, till like up to GCSE’s – it’s compulsory, like everyone does a bit of it. So I thought it was – that was like a bit of a taster and I liked it, like making things – I thought that was quite interesting, so I thought I’d carry on. If I’m enjoying it I might as well carry on.

Interviewer:	Yeah. OK, do you think anything influenced you to do it? Did you have any careers advice before you decided to go to university?

Erm, well we had these like – we were able to do these little tests things where we’d try and find out what careers we’ve get. Mine was a little bit creative, so they were saying like you could be a designer. That was on the list and I was thinking, oh that sounds quite nice.

Interviewer:	OK, so what about your family – have they been supportive?

Yeah, they’ve been supportive but I wouldn’t say they’ve influenced me as such as. My sister – she’s physiotherapist so she hadn’t done design, she didn’t really like design and my mum doesn’t either.

Interviewer:	So they were just happy with whatever you wanted to do?

Yeah.

Interviewer:	Did you ever consider studying anything else at University?

Erm, not really cos like – because of the ‘A’ levels I did, erm I did Geography and Physics as well, I didn’t think that I would do either of those, so I thought I quite enjoy design, so it’s kind of like what I thought I’d go into, if I had an ‘A’ level in it, it helps me out.

Interviewer:	What do you think it is about Design & Technology that appeals to you?

I like the creative side definitely more than the technology bit. Erm, I like the sort of – it’s nice to know I’ve got a course where I can do a bit of drawing and it’s not just like all essays all the time, so I like that side of it.

Interviewer:	OK, how did you decide to come to [this university]?

Erm, it probably the best university I looked at for design, because what I was looking for in the first place was Product Design. And they – they do like Product Design here but it’s different to what I was looking for – I wasn’t looking for sort of engineering courses but it is here, its kind of really technical here, so instead of that I picked Industrial Design here and just – it’s just got a really good reputation for design andI knew people who’d been here so….

Interviewer:	Ok. Are you going on a placement?

I’m trying to. I haven’t heard anything.

Interviewer:	OK. When you chose the course, did you know that you wanted to do a sandwich course?

Yeah. I put myself down for a sandwich, because some people don’t – they change their minds but I thought no, I’d like a sandwich.

Interviewer:	OK, we’ll talk a bit more about that later on. When you decided to do Design and Technology at University, did you realise that it was so male dominated?

Yes, cos it was at my school. Cos I was at a girls’ school but erm where they – when I began sixth form they actually began to erm make it joint because there was a boys school in my town, so we were like the first year to have a joint sixth form (yeah). So when I did design there I was one of 5 girls, out of more than 10 boys, 15 boys. So I was already starting to feel like it’s more male dominated, and like a few of the girls dropped out, so I was the only one in my set with just boys and the other girls were put together.

Interviewer:	Ok, do you think that coming from a girls’ school you’re encouraged more than maybe other girls are to do Design & Technology.

Maybe. I think because erm when you choose choices – you are in very small sets, er just doing design and girls and then I think only a few of us went on to do ‘A’ levels. The teacher kind of encouraged it. They said that’s what I want to do and they said, don’t be discouraged because it might be a lot of boys and things like that, so…

Interviewer:	Did it ever bother you then that there weren’t that many women?

No, not really cos – I just – I think it’s just the same really. I can see some people would be affected by that but (??) not me.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that more women should be encouraged to do design & technology?

I think so. As a subject, I liked it at ‘A’ level, but I can see why it’s not everyone’s type of thing. They wouldn’t like sort of making things as such, but I liked that bit. I think if it – you know you get a lot of girls like now, at my school now, because they know it’s a joint sixth form, they might turn away from it – they might think oh it’s just boys, I don’t want to be in with boys on my own. 

Interviewer:	Do you think that’s the main reason?

I think it could be one of them, yeah.

Interviewer:	Do you think that women are given the information to understand exactly what is involved in design & technology or do you think they maybe think oh I wouldn’t like to do that – it’s dirty, horrible?

Yeah, I think it has got a bit of a – sort of – they don’t tell you as much because they don’t think there’ll be that many girls, so it’s not quite – like they get more boys because they probably tell them more about it – the boys – more than the girls, yeah.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think then could be done to encourage more girls?

They could make it like a big factor you know – they should make it like really equal, like trying to get – like encourage the girls by saying to them it’s a really, really good course and if you like creative things and making things, it’s a good thing to do and don’t be scared that like, you know, cos’ it should say we’re trying to change it now.

Interviewer:	OK. What characteristics then do you think make a good designer?

Erm, I think if you’re really like structured in your thinking, you have to like really broaden – cos like, when you design things you have to sort of – you’ve got restrictions but you’ve got to work – work your way round them, see how you can like flex them out and make the designs good (yeah). If everyone sticks at the same thing then by the end of that, everyone’s got the same thing, but a good design is something that’s slightly different and you know, that makes it more special, if that makes sense.

Interviewer:	Would you say any characteristics about being a good designer are more male characteristics or more female characteristics?

Erm, a lot of people say it’s something about the brain – how the male use one side more than the other and that’s the key to sort of drawing and special thinking but that’s kind of – I don’t know if that’s true or not because obviously we do get a lot of women that are fine with all those things but erm – I just – you see it as like boys kind of the more technical they just seem to like enjoy it more, or just choose to do it more than girls. Girls choose different things, probably.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that there are any advantages or disadvantages of being a woman designer?

I don’t say there would be any disadvantages or advantages as such. I mean it changes for each person (yeah). I wouldn’t say like if you had a boy and a girl, then the girl would definitely be bright at this – better at this. Generally I don’t know – it’s just like erm boys probably see girls as like not going to make things very well. They’re just not going to deal with these kind of things as such. But they shouldn’t say that because like you both learn to do them like in your course, so…

Interviewer:	Do you think that girls may think they have to work twice as hard to actually prove that they can…?

Yeah, sometimes because my friend (name) she did design. She had – she has arthritis in her hands, so the teacher was saying to her that erm you might not be able to deal with the course, which she really wanted to do it and she proved herself by when she had problems she just carried on, so she worked extra hard to get that credit. And I think when you see it (lost words).

Interviewer:	Some other people that I’ve spoken to on your course have said that because you’re a girl, it’s sometimes easier to get help if you’re stuck on something?

(Laughs) Yeah, sometimes because the lecturers, like there are quite a few male ones and, but I think they’re still not quite used to teaching with girls. I think probably because like – like a few years ago it would just be mainly boys and they’re used to that and it’s changing now, so there’s more girls and so they don’t quite know how to treat you and they’re just a bit cautious maybe. They were like that in my school as well – the teachers, you know, because I was the only girl in my set as I say and no, if I had any problems they’d be willing to help cos maybe they thought I wouldn’t know as much (laughs) so they’d be extra helpful.

Interviewer:	Do you think that is a good thing or do you find it at all patronising?

Erm, well the good thing is if you want the help and you can get the help, that’s fine but I can see how some people might see it that I suppose they sort of – mollycoddle you – I don’t mind.

Interviewer:	OK, talking a bit about the course then, has it been what you expected it to be?

Not quite. (laughs) it’s been a lot of harder than I thought it would be. It’s a lot – they put emphasis on the technology cos when we first came they were saying it’s industrial design and technology, it’s not like just industrial design and then the technology bit. It’s like, you know, design & technology together. And it’s like they – they see you drawing and then they sort of criticise your drawing and say you can’t draw right, so you start to feel a bit like hmm, maybe I’m not quite as good on this course. You see other people doing it and it comes really naturally (yeah) because they tell us to sketch things and then the way of sketching that they like – like really fast but accurate and I had a bit of a problem – a few problems with that and that was done and it’s not gone quite exactly as I thought It’s different to my ‘A’ levels (yeah) – definitely.

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think have been the best and the worst things about the course so far?

The worst thing I would say was doing computer design – CAD, because I’ve never done it before – ever and they start you off, some of – in the first IT lesson we had I think we were learning how to send an email. So it really was a good start, cos I know how to do that – you know, carry on from there and it might be quite, quite OK, you know. But then like they’d completely skipped onto this new erm programme like for engineers, that we use mostly, and we can design things on that, but I’d never used it before and the – the menus are like really weird and hard to get hold of (yeah) so I had like really – a really hard time like getting the grasp of that, but you do get the help that – like, the lecturer that we had for that he wasn’t particularly that helpful and a lot of people complained about it, so like trying to do an assignment, you’d just kind of help each other out and there’s me trying to get the hang of it and each time you have a bit more work you get, like a better grasp of it but I found that quite hard – I still do (yeah). But I don’t know what the best thing – the best thing I enjoy. I do like erm a module I’m doing now, it’s called Product Analysis and Artefacts and that’s a really creative one. Like they don’t ask for technology, all like you design something - they don’t ask like how would it work? They don’t ask precisely what electronics have you got? And it’s just kind of like – it’s, it’s – I think it’s more fun that way because you get to be like creative and think like innovative things, and we look at like, like shops and we look at like brands and products and it’s that side of design that I prefer like the more creative, thinking side instead of – yeah, cos like I like drawing but I don’t say that I’m the best and I wouldn’t like to draw all the time either (yeah) cos there’s another module called Styling and they do a lot of like rendering and things like that and I’m thinking hmm, I don’t like that too much.

Interviewer:	Do you find that on your course a lot of the girls go towards like the creative modules and the lads go more to the technical stuff?

Yeah, cos like we’ve got – we’ve got electronics and mechanics modules (yeah) and for the second years you do options and you get to choose 2 modules that you choose. And I’ve chosen mechanics first and then this creative products one. I went into mechanics and they’re like not very many girls – it’s a very small group anyway, but I didn’t like that module so I changed, cos I couldn’t really like handle the working with technical bits. I thought I might try but I couldn’t and I didn’t want to like lose out on a module so I changed, but erm in electronics as well, I don’t think there are many girls doing that. Definitely the girls kind of choose the more creative.

Interviewer:	How many girls are there on your course?

I’d say roughly about a quarter to two thirds, about – there’s definitely more than half of boys, I reckon.

Interviewer:	Ok, are you pleased that you chose this course then?

Yeah, yeah definitely.

Interviewer:	Have you been taught by any female lecturers?

Yeah we have – we’ve had a couple, I think, one or two. We had one when I was in the second year and she takes the sustainable design module which is one I’ve chosen as well and then last year we had erm I think we had a few but they weren’t kind of design lecturers. I think that we had like materials people – that they were like mainly materials, they’d just teach us for a few – so they would be mainly male, not very many females at all.

Interviewer:	Do you – have you noticed any sort of difference in say style of teaching between and male and female lecturers?

Yeah. This new lady called (name), that we have for sustainable design, she’s really like friendly and open and you can like – it’s easy to learn things and you can just chat about things just broadly, which helps quite a lot but whereas some of the male lecturers they are not quite so friendly and you kind of go to the lecture and learn things and that’s it - you don’t have to talk to them at all. Whereas some other ones are much more friendlier but I think…

Interviewer:	Do you ever think that’s an age thing, do you think?

Yeah, it could be, in a way, but I think I don’t know if you could call it like just the women are more friendly and the men not quite so much, but it just – it changes for every person (yeah) so like we had some male lecturers that are like, they’re really friendly and helpful, others are just in their character not to be or it is an age thing as well, like some older ones maybe they don’t understand younger people.

Interviewer:	OK. Would you find it encouraging to have more female lecturers?

I think it would help. But I mean they don’t tell you as you like apply for the course, you won’t know what lecturers you’ll have, but I think, in a way, it could sort of encourage girls a bit more. They’d feel like on a par with other females so they’d find it more comfortable if they had more females, maybe help them settle in more easily and things.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the lecturers treat the students all equally?

Mmm, some do – some might not (laughs). I dunno – some lecturers are a bit touchy, if you get on the wrong side of them or don’t know how they are, like if you ask too many questions they might get annoyed with you, you know, if you don’t ask enough they might get annoyed with you. It’s just – I don’t know – it depends on each person.

Interviewer:	Yeah, you don’t think that they treat the female and male students differently at all?

There’s this one assistant in our department and he is known for helping girls out more than boys (OK) and we were doing an electronics project last year and I had a friend, a girl and a boy and the boy went up to ask him sort of questions, for some help and he said, look in this book. And the girl asked the same questions and he did all the stuff for her like looked up all these things, off these sheets and things and helped her out and went to check on her and stuff. So I think he was a bit more helpful obviously to the girls than the boys – and the boys got a bit angry.

Interviewer:	OK, have you got a personal tutor?

Yes.

Interviewer:	Are they male or female?

Female this year, and male last year.

Interviewer:	OK, how have you found that? Do you prefer having a female personal tutor, do you think they’re more approachable?

Yeah, I think – I mean I’m not bothered as such cos my lecturer, my tutor last year he was really friendly, very helpful when I asked him all these questions and (name) is the same this year. She – I mean she’s just generally quite a nice person, I think, so she’s just that way – so I think she’ll try to help them as much as she can, whereas erm some people say their tutors – like my friend (name), she’s got a male tutor and he’s – I think last year it was, he wasn’t very helpful at all, like she wouldn’t bother going to tutorials or meeting him. If she had any problems she’d just go to someone else.

Interviewer:	Yeah, OK. Is there anything or anyone that you’d say has been the biggest influence on you since you started the course?

Yeah, we had a lecturer last year called (name) but she’s left now and we’re all really sad that she’s left because erm she’s really wacky as such. She’s really into design – you can tell from the way she speaks. She’s really enthusiastic about just like certain products, because she’s known for just buying a product, and she’ll look at it, and not use it, like a kettle, like a designed kettle. She won’t use it, she’ll just touch it and just like show people and I think that’s really nice – it like encourages people to become like, like more enthusiastic about their course and design (yeah) which is sort of not just doing what’s on the course but actually being interested in it.

Interviewer:	That’s quite inspiring.

Yeah, because then you don’t get bored, you don’t want to like think all the time oh I’m going to uni to do this. Whereas, just like it just comes naturally just when you’re at home, or around town, you just – you are naturally a designer. You think oh my God, look at this and it’s good because she took the module for erm the product analysis and artefacts and she just lets you become really creative and she’ll encourage you to think like – not straight and narrow but just completely crazy, which is like – it helps in design, in like designing things and she’s left us and it’s like oh no (laughs)

Interviewer:	I heard that some of the lads didn’t take to her quite as much as the girls?

Yeah. Yeah, cos they thought she was a bit too mad and they’d not be quite so enthusiastic like going to museums and looking at things, they’d just be like it’s just this, this, this, but you know if I get projects off them, why can’t they put up – yeah, they don’t like her as much as the girls, I don’t think.

Interviewer:	That’s interesting. Have you had to do a lot of group work?

Yeah, we do quite a lot of group work.

Interviewer:	Do you like doing group work?

I do actually. I’ve been quite lucky because erm the people either that you’ve been put with, or that you pick yourself, when I’ve been put in the groups, my people have been like we’ve all been helpful, and friendly, and willing to work – like the boys and girls and that’s been fine but I’ve heard a few people who’ve said their groups have been not good to help them work with, because some people just aren’t willing to help other people – they just do their bit and they just leave other people, even if they find it hard they won’t help them out. I don’t know if that works quite so well.

Interviewer:	Do you think that men and women bring different characteristics to group work?

Yeah. No it’s – to a limit I think but it’s just cos like each person thinks differently and when you work together, each person has like a different point – there’s spots I think they’ll bring that out. So erm, and then some of them projects, I’d say like if you had boys and girls, the boys do tend to do the technical things – they like notice things and like say you have to make something and you have to do it – like use machines and things, they just seem to know how to do things better than the girls (yeah). I mean some girls might not know so much – other girls are fine but…

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think might be the benefits of doing group work then?

Erm, I reckon the fact that you have different views and you know, you just – when discussing it’s much easier, you don’t – if you just like, there’s 2 people you’d say maybe just think of the same thing and you wouldn’t spot something else (yeah). If you’ve got a lot of people you just like have a lot wider view of things and then also, if you’ve got lots of work to share out then it’s like you don’t have to do everything by yourself. It’s shares out all the stress and all the worry and getting it together should be alright.

Interviewer:	Do you think that getting different views is particularly important on the course that you’re doing?

Mm, I think that – yeah, cos they do – I mean well projects they just make sure that their own groups and they do stress that like work together in a group and you’ll say, you know, you’ve got to help each other and I think getting the different vies is quite helpful cos you just get better work that way.

Interviewer:	Do you think that the group work that you’ve done will be a good experience for when you go to work in the industry?

Yeah definitely because we’ve been doing our CV’s recently (laughs) and people will say put down group work, teamwork you know, because when you become – when you like graduate and you want to find a job it’s very important to be a – to be able to work with other people, people you might not know, or like, you know, when you first start a job you can’t like not speak to people. If you don’t know them you can’t just like wait a couple of months, get to know them and then work’s fine, it is important to be able to like – like agree with someone, even if you don’t see their sort of side – you don’t think exactly the same, but you try and – you don’t rule things out. (Yeah) You’ve got to be like fair.

Interviewer:	OK. Do you think that there are any aspects, like the teaching or advice that you’ve had, that will help you when you go on placement?

Erm, (laughs) I don’t know. There’s still an emphasis on the group work thing and erm I don’t know what….

Interviewer:	Do you think that you’ll use the technical skills that you’ve learnt as much as the generic skills like the group work?

Yeah, I think all the – depending on what type of placement you choose because you’re choosing yourselves (yeah). Erm, I’ve sort of leaned away from all the ones that ask for technical things just cos I don’t want to be stuck, for like a year, doing something I’d be bored with or not think I’d be able to manage too well. So, but obviously you’re doing placements that are more creative than technical but you do get – mostly, they would ask for a bit of both – for design placements especially, because like being modern times then it’s like there are – people are using more computers, so to have computer skills and maybe not quite so much computer designing on programmes, just sort of basic computer skills like Word and programmes like that, it’s helpful, I think. So you can’t just like be pen and paper and drawing, you’ve got to know how to do things on computers.

Interviewer:	Yeah. OK. Why do you want to go on placement then?

I thought it would be a really good way of getting work experience, because people say you can do these things in the summer but often they’re not paying things, so I like to work in the summer and get a bit of money for the year, so I tend to not apply for like design placements on my summer, so I tend to have a bit of like time to relax as well. And so, if you did like a placement, you get to like see how design works in industry, like it’s completely different to designing on a course, like getting a project set. I mean you might get projects set like in your job, but working differently you know – they leave everything to yourself, like you have to do everything, organise everything by yourself, and if you’re in a group you’ve got to do everything together, you’re not gonna have like a lecturer coming in and making sure you’ve done things (yeah). So I think it’s gonna be very different and strange.

Interviewer:	Has anyone particularly encouraged or discouraged you from going on placement at all?

I’ve spoken to a few 3rd years – I’ve been asking why they haven’t gone on a placement (right) erm and they’ve basically said they want to get like the final year over with – they want to get University over with, so they can carry – like go out into the world and see what they want to do. Erm, and I was – I’m kind of like – I’ve applied for – to go on a placement course, but I’ve been thinking like at the end of last year, thinking I don’t know if I want one – if I want one, cos like if you get like a year’s experience that would be really good but I’ve always been like scared that like you’d lose some skills, like if your placement didn’t have emphasis on like computer design as such, by the time you came back you might forget everything – yeah. Or, if you don’t like sketch all the time, when you come back and you’ve got to do some sketching, it might be like really rusty (yeah) and also like if you just get a placement and it’s not quite what you expected, then I’d be like wasting time as such, like you wouldn’t be enjoying it, whereas you just want to get your course finished with, so…

Interviewer:	Have you spoken to anyone who’s been on placement?

Erm, well I went – I applied to one at [company], which is in [place] and they came to give us a talk and they had two of the people that were on our course on placement there, this year. So we all asked them questions and spoke to them and they seemed to really enjoy that one. I mean they must have like wanted to do it (yeah) cos you can tell that they really like – their projects that they’ve been set, they seem to like really enjoy them, because the placement at [company] it’s like – you don’t draw things yourself, you don’t design things yourself but you work with like a design team and you do the drawings and creative thing. So you do have part – like parts of creative thinking, but a lot of the other things that they do is like administration, they have to ring things like printers up and check things and when we had this talk with them a lot of people are saying it’s not their type of thing, they want to be like creative all the time, whereas I think that that’s like exactly my type of thing cos I like being creative but not all the time like. I’m fine with doing anything, like talking on the phone.

Interviewer:	Yeah, it’s quite broad (exactly). OK, what has attracted you to the companies that you have been applying to?

I haven’t applied to that many (laughs) but erm when I’ve been looking for them, er just the ones that say like quite creative, and almost like quite relaxed (yeah). Not really very formal and there’s a lot of ones that are like really technical, like into manufacturing and (yeah) machines and things like that and I don’t – I’ll stay away from those ones because I don’t want to do them. I don’t want to be like working on a computer all the time, so I’ve stayed away from technical.

Interviewer:	Have you looked at other things like training opportunities, or pay, or location?

Er, I’ve looked at location cos for a while I didn’t know what I wanted to do, I didn’t know whether I was going for a placement or not (yeah) cos I didn’t really want to go for a placement and have to live somewhere by myself, cos I know of someone from around the University who’s gone on an engineering placement, he’s in Yorkshire, by himself, with no-one around and they’re all old people. He’s got really bored and I didn’t like the sound of that, like it turns me off it, but quite a lot, so I was thinking if I was looking for a placement I’d look for ones like round here, cos I live only an hour away from [university town] so either in [university town], I could stay here, or like round home and I could still be like near [this university] where my friends are. So erm I’m thinking OK, maybe I’ll do that and then, all my friends started to get houses and I’m like thinking OK, what if I don’t get a placement? I might be stuck for somewhere to live (yeah) and like have to finish the final year and not have anyone like my friends to live with, so I’m a little bit panicky. So I decided – I thought I’d live in [university town], so I’ve got a house now (OK) so when I’m looking for placements now, they’re definitely around [university area], like where I can commute to. So I’ve restricted myself to that. Erm, pay – I haven’t looked at like quite a bit. I mean obviously it’s nice to get paid but I’m thinking like, if – if you get paid that’s a bonus already like, because they’ll be paying you something and you’re getting like good experience out of work if you choose the right one, so I haven’t worried too much about pay – I haven’t looked for a high salary and just aimed for those, I haven’t looked at that too much.

Interviewer:	OK, have you done much research into the companies then?

Erm, I mean I haven’t applied to many placements; I haven’t looked for too many because I don’t think I would be disappointed if I didn’t get one, so I haven’t looked into different companies too much. I think maybe, if I got an interview, then, at that point, maybe I’d look into them and …

Interviewer:	See if you did really want to work there?

Yeah I haven’t like found companies and then applied to them, like I haven’t looked at things that way. I’ve just looked for ones that have been advertised.

Interviewer:	OK, yeah, that’s fine. Has the University been very involved in trying to help you find a placement?

Erm, we have a lecturer who’s like in place – in charge of placements and he sends emails now and again of like placements that have been like advertised (yeah) so you get to see those ones. But most of them I’m not interested in and they’re like really far away or really technical. So I just – don’t know, so they have, in that sense, like emailed you now and again but no-one else says anything else and it’s just up to you basically to find one, cos erm we had a talk on getting placements but erm compared to the other people, all my friends on other courses who are doing placements, they had talks really like early (yeah) and ours was really late so I was thinking how are we supposed to get them now? But apparently design placements come a bit later.

Interviewer:	Yeah, I’ve heard that. I mean not many of the people that I’ve spoken to on your course have got placements yet.

Yeah, exactly, so …

Interviewer:	What is your placement co-ordinator called?

Erm, [name]. 

Interviewer:	Thank you. OK, do you think that the University could do more then, to help you find a placement? What would you like them to do?

Well, I would like them to help more but they do – they do say to you it is completely up to you to find one, so I wasn’t expecting that much help, to be honest. Erm, like I think the careers service is really helpful, but it’s up to you to go there yourself and they do mention it, like on our course, the lecturers do say there’s a careers service, so I think they’re a lot more helpful. If you go there they can give you more advice but then they’re not like specialised in design placements, they’re just more general – like just general advice on placements, because I went to have my CV checked and erm she was looking at all these things and she was saying maybe, you know, it’s different if you’re a designer, you could like make all the fonts a bit jazzy or something, but I was like asking – I wasn’t sure whether to or not, like is it supposed to be kept formal or am I allowed to be creative? And she wasn’t really sure what to say (yeah), and I was like hmm and that was like that’s what the personal tutor’s for – you know if you have any questions on placements, you can talk to them. I mean you can talk to like any lecturer you want to – you just go and like go to their office but you – there’s some you wouldn’t think of going to, you’d just go to some specific ones – ones that are friendly, helpful and you think they’ll know what to say, kind of thing.

Interviewer:	OK, what sorts of things are you hoping to get out of the placement then?

Money (laughs), well erm hopefully just something – I’ll find something that I really enjoy and then I’ll know that’s the kind of thing I want to go for, after I graduate (yeah) cos at the moment, erm well I don’t think like I want to be an industrial designer as such. Er, I’m interested in design things but not – I don’t want to be like really technical and in just like industrial things. So it’s more like a broad range of design and I’m not quite sure which I’d like to go for.

Interviewer:	Yeah, so hopefully it might help make your mind up?

Yeah, cos’ like if you went for a job and then you found like a few things that you’d like to do and other things that you didn’t like doing, then you get like a better idea of what kind of job to apply for so hopefully that’ll help and like just generally getting inside the work routine (yeah) instead of being at University cos like our course is quite hard but it is still quite flexible, so you have like mornings off or afternoons off (yeah) whereas in a job you wouldn’t have that and you’d have to learn to just like have the evenings off and have the weekends off (yeah). And the people I spoke to on the [company] placement, they said they don’t have any work to do after they finish their job, which is – I think is good. But you see other people on tv and films and stuff and they’re always working all the time and I’m like, oh, it’s just like being at University – no. 

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that you’ll be able to use what you learn on placement, when you come back for your final year?

Erm, depending what placement you have. If you’ve gone for like one that’s a bit designed and not so much – I don’t know how helpful that would be. But then just the working side of having a job, that would help you, but after graduating. But erm, I think the organisation would be quite useful because like, when you’re working on a placement it’s like a job (yeah) and it’s a lot more independent than like at University. I mean at University they do expect you to do things yourself but they will help if you really want it. So I think like that way you can like more organised within yourself, making sure you do things.

Interviewer:	OK, if you do go on placement, what do you think that you’ll be most looking forward to and most worried about?

Erm, I think I’ll be looking forward to like just new things – like new things to do with design, like on my course it’s like pretty much the same thing, whereas like you can see what else there is out there (yeah). Erm, what am I not looking forward to? Er, coming back and forgetting things (laughs).

Interviewer:	OK, what do you think are the main ways that being at work will differ from being at University?

Probably hours, like having to work from 9 to 5. Well, some places might not be that but they’ll be about that – yeah. Erm, it just – having to like, like you’ve got to make sure you do everything, cos like here, if you don’t do something, you just fail yourself – you know you haven’t done it OK, that’s fair enough, whereas if you’ve got work for other people, and they’re waiting for your work, if you haven’t like done it till the deadline and you hold them up and they might hold someone else up. I think that’s quite important and then like you’ve got to make sure you do what’s asked of you – I think that’s really important.

Interviewer:	OK, in terms of your career then, what do you think you’ll be in, in say 5 years time?

Erm, hopefully something I really enjoy to do with design. Er, cos like we look at sort of a broad range of like product design, we don’t sort of look at just electronic products and things like that. I’m more interested in things like – like toy design really (yeah) and just things that aren’t like – you have to think oh, where does the battery go and stuff like that, it’s like more creative things l think. Hopefully, something that’s quite relaxed with design and technology but not – not engineering as such.

Interviewer:	OK, what about in 10 years time?

Oooh, erm I’m not sure. Maybe I’ll have changed my mind about design by then and want to do something completely different – I don’t know. I’ve always been interested in like erm dolls, say like doll set design. I’ve always thought that would be like a really cool job to do (yeah) but I don’t know. That’s not like the design I’ve been studying as such, that’s kind of like real life design and you sort of like (its different?). I don’t know if I’d like – that’d be really like interesting to look into but it’s one of those things you don’t think you could ever be unless you like really, really worked for it. I don’t know. It just seems really unobtainable.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good in design and technology?

I think so because like with the things you learn on my course, if you are more interested in creative things you’ve got that from my course and then if by the end of it you’ve got a job that’s quite creative, then suddenly they go you do need a bit of technology like working with computers, then definitely I’ve got that like just all the different things on my course. I’d better do it because we have like drawing things but in the first year we had a module that we had to write essays for, so it’s not like we haven’t done essay writing (yeah) we have done a bit of it and had help with like doing references and things like that. So I think our broad – our range is – our course is – it’s a lot more different to other courses like, they’d be like really specialised in what they’re doing, whereas we have quite a lot different aspects – yeah, a big variety of things.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the career prospects are good once you’re in the industry, fo climbing the career ladder?

(laughs) Er, you – I think you – it’s quite good but it’s a lot of learning still, I think, in our industry because like depending on where you go there’s certain ways of doing things and learning things (yeah) so you’d have to like get used to that way of thinking, cos everything’s different, like if you’re technical or creative then you’d have to think differently for that way and then you’d like to work that way. I don’t think it’d be that easy to get like really successful – it depends on what you choose.

Interviewer:	Do you think that – that is the route that you will want to do?

Er, possibly – if I find something that I really enjoy, then I’ll work at hard at that (yeah) – I think I’d like to be like quite successful in that.

Interviewer:	OK, would you do anything differently if you went through all your career choices that you’ve made so far?

Erm, I always thought I should do Art. I always worried that like if I had done Art erm would I be good? Because before I did – chose my courses for University erm all I’d done was design and I’d done Art when I was like small but it’s not like GCSE Art or ‘A’ level Art and I never did those – like I was worried I wasn’t quite creative as much as other people and I was like, I like to draw but I didn’t know if I was good. So like, before I came to Uni I did like a few Art things like I did like er natural drawing and things like that to get myself like more arty and such, cos when we came here there was a lot of people who’d done Art and they were like just natural in drawing and things like that, whereas I have to work a bit. I don’t – as I said they expect kind of like a way of drawing and they’re just sort of criticising and I’m like, I’m trying. It doesn’t come naturally to me, because I didn’t – I should’ve done Art (yeah) and I think I would’ve like really enjoyed Art though, because it’s like murals and things, you know drawing obviously but looking at History of Art and I think that’s really interesting cos we did a module on the History of Design, which is like design history and things like that and I found that really interesting, like the basics of design now and its confluence sort of thing. I find that interesting.

Interviewer:	OK, what 5 words would you use to describe the characteristics of the design industry?

Hard-working, erm sort of work like team work – kind of like group – like you have to be able to work together and get, yeah. Erm, conscientious, erm, can’t think of a word for it but like keeping to a deadline kind of erm organised (yeah). That’s pretty much that.

Interviewer:	Would you describe it as masculine?

Erm, I almost want to but I don’t want to because like you don’t want to think of it that way. If you think – you want to think it’s changing and not that way, but you could definitely say it’s a little bit masculine, more than feminine definitely.

Interviewer:	When you say it’s masculine, do you think that is just to do with the numbers of men that do the subject or do you think it’s about more than that?

Erm, I think that affects it quite a lot but I think it is a bit more than that cos just – the general stereotype of like men and women you’d think men would be – they just generally would choose to do design more than women and just things that people think about then like being able to make things and think technically. I think you can see it that way, it just seems more suited to like men than women (yeah) and so it would be masculine that way. Like say – like nursing, people would think that’s strange to have men to be a nurse, because they’d see that as more feminine – like women are caring and men are just making things (laughs) cos I think just like, from like years and years and years ago just what men used to do and what women couldn’t do, that obviously still remains slightly, strangely enough. It is changing but just the general like almost reputation of what men would do like little boys would go out into the shed with their dads and (yeah) build things out of wood, whereas women would cook in the kitchen. It’s just like – just how – like maybe men have naturally evolved to be able to do design and obviously women, who might do it, it’s just because they have an interest – maybe they’re not quite so suited.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the situation will improve for women?

Yeah, I think so cos erm, from my school – cos we’ve now got joint sixth form, there is a lot more equal – like the girls can now do ‘A’ level design (yeah), like with the boys and just the same as the boys, because for GCSE we did graphic design whereas the boys did like design with materials, which is a lot – it is what design and technology is like now, especially in my course now we do a lot of materials. So when I first went into it, the girls weren’t quite the same as the boys (yeah) but now you’ve got like an equal opportunity to learn that side of design for ‘A’ level and then go onto that type of thing if you want to. It’s becoming a lot more equal.

Interviewer:	OK, do you think that the fact that the industry is male dominated will ever cause you any problems, trying to get jobs or the way you’re treated when you’re working, or anything like that?

Erm, I think in some places it can be but erm obviously there are going to be women in the industry now, erm because there has been for a few years but I found – I find that some people are saying like even though, they’ve still got problems with it, like they do have like – like people that’ve been treated unfairly. There’s just like some people that are old-fashioned and they are that way.

Interviewer:	Does that worry you at all?

It does slightly like I don’t want to be put down, cos’ you know, you’re a woman. But it does kind of like – it’s at the back of my mind, it can happen – just because some people might be that way. So, I hope it doesn’t.

Interviewer:	OK, that’s everything, thank you very much.

turns.text: OK. What characteristics then do you think make a good designer?
